units.title: Instruction pipelines, branches and SIMD
outcomes: Explain pipeline overlap, instruction dependencies and branch recovery without equating clock cycles with instructions.
Identify SIMD lanes, loop tails and a loop-carried dependency in compiler output.
Separate a compiler's vectorization decision from evidence of a runtime speedup.
units.why: Assume Programming's layout-alignment-locality and profiling-benchmarking units. Here the mechanism is instruction execution: dependencies, speculation and SIMD determine which work can overlap before the kernel or storage enters the picture.

next.note: Explain why wider arithmetic still has to wait for data.

study.title: Pipelining & Performance
study.locator: Iron Law of Processor Performance; Pipelined Processors; Performance of Pipelined Processors; Latency vs. Throughput; Hazards
study.depth: Use the ideal five-stage calculation and the control-hazard example. Do not transfer its CPI or stage count to the i9, or follow the textbook pointer into full processor design.

study.title: Loop vectorization and its limits
study.locator: Usage; Diagnostics; Features: Loops with unknown trip count, Runtime Checks of Pointers, Reductions, If Conversion and Partial unrolling during vectorization
study.depth: Stop before Epilogue Vectorization. Skip historical Performance charts; they are not measurements of this machine.

focus: Pipeline overlap improves throughput, not necessarily the latency of one instruction. Dependencies limit overlap; a wrong branch prediction discards speculative work.
Instruction count, CPI and clock period all enter execution time. Out-of-order execution schedules ready work but must preserve architectural behavior.
SIMD widens independent operations. Tails, alias checks, calls and recurrences constrain the generated loop; unrolling is not itself SIMD.
If conversion can replace branches. Inspect the executable before calling an input-order timing difference a branch-prediction effect.
units.reproduce: From a blank C file, write noinline bump(uint32_t *a, unsigned n) with a[i] += 1u for i=0..n-1, and noinline chain with a[i] += a[i-1] for i=1..n-1. In main initialize 1031 elements to i, call bump, sum into uint64_t and print it, then call chain and print a[1030]. Compile with clang -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 -Rpass=loop-vectorize -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize, and again with -fno-vectorize -fno-slp-vectorize. Run both with taskset -c 2. Both print 531996 twice. On Clang 21.1.8, bump vectorizes with eight uint32_t lanes and chain does not; confirm packed additions and the scalar tail with objdump -d. This is a correctness and instruction observation, not a timing claim.
traps: Counting SIMD lanes as a promised speedup. Loads, stores, dependencies and loop overhead still consume resources.
Using signed overflow or floating-point reassociation as an exact correctness oracle. Use unsigned arithmetic here; floating-point reductions need a stated error criterion.
Timing a loop the compiler folded away, or attributing branch misses to source-level if statements that became branchless code.

selfTest.q: In an ideal five-stage pipeline with no stalls, how many cycles complete ten instructions?
selfTest.a: Four fill cycles plus ten completions: 14 cycles. This is a model, not a measurement of the host CPU.

selfTest.q: Why does chain not have the same independent lanes as bump?
selfTest.a: Iteration i needs the value written by iteration i-1. A simple widening would read the wrong predecessor; a different algorithm such as a parallel scan is needed.

selfTest.q: Does a vectorization remark prove the vector loop ran for a particular call?
selfTest.a: No. A small length, tail or runtime alias check can select a scalar path. Inspect the call's inputs and generated control flow.

selfTest.q: Can a predictable branch be cheaper than computing both arms?
selfTest.a: Yes. Prediction can avoid unnecessary work. Which version wins depends on the generated code and workload and must be measured.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a correctness-checked scalar/vectorized kernel, dependency and branch variants, saved assembly, and pinned repeated measurements with compiler flags and warm-up state.
units.stopWhen: Both builds agree on the checksum and recurrence endpoint, and you can mark the vector lanes, scalar tail and dependency in the executable without promising a speedup.

fit.note: The selected OS pool does not locate pipelines or SIMD at working depth. Cornell supplies the pipeline model and LLVM supplies current, executable vectorization guidance; the mini-project supplies performance practice.

units.title: Caches, working sets, bandwidth and NUMA
outcomes: Explain cache-line fills, coherence and false sharing separately from language-level synchronization.
Measure a traversal-order change with a fixed working set and a correctness oracle.
Estimate useful bytes and line traffic with units, and distinguish bandwidth from dependent-load latency.
Explain CPU affinity and NUMA page placement without claiming remote-memory measurements on a one-node host.
units.why: Assume Programming's layout-alignment-locality unit, including its AoS/SoA experiment. This unit moves to cache ownership, working-set regimes and physical placement rather than repeating that layout comparison.

next.note: Add translation and residency to the memory-access path.
Measure cache-line ownership traffic under actual multicore contention.

study.title: The Memory Hierarchy and Why Latency Matters
study.locator: CPU Caches through Memory Capacity vs. Memory Speed; A Simple Locality Experiment
study.depth: Correct the experiment before running it: its unmodified static matrix is all zero and GCC can remove the loops. Initialize every element to (row+column)&255 and declare the matrix volatile so both access orders remain. This measures scalar volatile traversal, not optimized application bandwidth.

study.title: Coherence and false sharing
study.locator: Cache Coherence vs. Memory Consistency; False Sharing: Independent Data, Shared Cache Line; True Sharing and False Sharing; Separating Frequently Written Data
study.depth: Leave atomics and the multicore benchmark to the concurrency section. A single-core-pinned run cannot demonstrate lines bouncing between cores.

study.title: NUMA placement vocabulary
study.locator: NUMA: Memory Locality through NUMA Problems in Backend Services
study.depth: Inspect topology only. This host has one NUMA node, so skip commands requiring node 1 and do not report a local/remote timing ratio.

focus: Read cpu2/cache/index*/{level,type,size,coherency_line_size,shared_cpu_list} under /sys/devices/system/cpu and run lscpu before estimating line traffic. Aggregate lscpu cache sizes are not per-core capacities.
A stream can overlap independent misses and use bandwidth; a pointer chain waits for each next address and exposes latency. Useful bytes/time is not automatically DRAM traffic/time.
Coherence coordinates writes to locations. It does not establish the language's cross-location publication order; false sharing is independent writers sharing one line.
Working-set fit, conflicts, prefetch, translation and frequency all affect a curve. CPU pinning does not relocate pages; NUMA distance values are not measured nanoseconds.
units.reproduce: Rebuild the corrected A Simple Locality Experiment from memory: a static volatile int matrix[4096][4096], initialized to (r+c)&255 before timing, with row-first and column-first sums into long long and CLOCK_MONOTONIC around each traversal. Build with gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra and run taskset -c 2 ./locality five times. Each traversal sums to 2139095040; the array is 64 MiB when sizeof(int)==4. Record all timings, kernel, CPU and GCC version, and note that initialization touched all pages but a 64 MiB array cannot be wholly warm in this host's 30 MiB LLC. Do not assume either traversal wins. Derive line utilization using the inspected line size, then explain why TLB behavior and volatile loads prevent this from being a pure DRAM-bandwidth benchmark.
traps: Turning a slower strided run into a cache-miss count. Timing alone cannot separate cache, TLB, prefetch and instruction effects.
Using perf c2c or system-wide counters despite host permissions. Keep optional counters to your own pinned process and user-space cycles/instructions; cpu_core and cpu_atom are separate PMUs.
Reporting NUMA remote latency from this machine. There is no second memory node to measure.

selfTest.q: For an aligned array of four-byte integers and an inspected 64-byte line, how much of each line does a stride-16 pass use?
selfTest.a: One integer, or 4/64 = 1/16 of the line, before any later reuse. This is useful-byte utilization, not a measured memory-traffic multiplier.

selfTest.q: Why can two race-free counters still contend in hardware?
selfTest.a: Separate counters can share one cache line. Writes on different cores repeatedly require ownership of that line even though neither counter has multiple writers.

selfTest.q: Does a working set smaller than cache capacity guarantee hits?
selfTest.a: No. Conflicts, competing code/data and other users of shared cache can evict lines; compulsory fills still occur.

selfTest.q: What can numactl --hardware establish on a one-node host?
selfTest.a: Visible CPUs, node membership and node capacity. It cannot supply an observed remote-memory penalty.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: working-set and stride sweeps across inspected cache capacities, a dependent pointer chase versus a stream, matched checksums, pinned five-repeat raw timings, and a topology note explicitly excluding remote NUMA claims.
units.stopWhen: Both traversal checksums agree, your evidence records topology and cache state, and you can explain useful-byte traffic, latency versus bandwidth and a hypothetical false-sharing layout without treating timing as causal proof.

fit.note: The selected pool lacks located cache/coherence/NUMA teaching. Three owned AlgoMaster hardware lessons fill that coverage gap; corrected traversal and the mini-project give measured practice.

units.title: Processes, system calls, fork, exec and scheduling
outcomes: Trace fork, exec and wait while identifying kernel-owned state and preserved process identity.
Distinguish a privilege-mode transition from a scheduler context switch.
Implement child launch and status collection with an explicit exec-failure path.
Predict ready, running and blocked transitions under a stated scheduling model.
units.why: Assume Programming's shell-processes-environment unit and its exit-status and trap exercises. Here you trace the kernel process model, not shell syntax, and make the launcher own every child it creates.

next.note: Give the child deliberate I/O and termination ownership.

study.title: Protected execution and scheduling
study.locator: Chapter 6, Sections 6.1 to 6.3; Chapter 7, Sections 7.1 to 7.2 and 7.6 to 7.8 (CPU Scheduling, linked from the book contents)
study.depth: Treat round robin as a model, not Linux's normal scheduler. A context switch can disturb cache/TLB locality; it does not necessarily flush every cache or every tagged TLB entry.

study.title: Linux process launch and switching
study.locator: What exec Replaces and What It Preserves; Encoded Wait Status; Handling an Interrupted Wait; Multithreaded fork Considerations; Failure Handling by Operation

study.title: Xv6 utilities: the exec task
study.locator: exec: adding -exec cmd to find; hints on fork, exec and wait
study.depth: Read and sketch the lifecycle only. RISC-V tools and QEMU are not installed here, so do not claim a make grade result. Leave full util-lab completion to a provisioned course environment.

focus: Fork creates a child with a different PID; successful exec replaces its address space while retaining its PID. Wait consumes an owned child's termination record.
System calls enter controlled kernel code. A call can return in the same task without any switch to another task; blocking or preemption can cause scheduling.
Ready is not running, and blocked is not merely low CPU usage. Linux's R status includes running and runnable tasks.
Response time and turnaround time answer different questions. A policy comparison needs arrivals, CPU bursts, I/O durations and switch assumptions.
units.reproduce: Write a single-threaded Python launcher using os.fork, os.execl and os.waitpid. In the child, os.write its PID before exec; execute /bin/sh with arguments -c 'echo

; exit 7'. The parent waits for that PID and decodes WIFEXITED/WEXITSTATUS. Repeat with /atlas-missing-executable, catching OSError in the child and calling os._exit(127). Run taskset -c 2 strace -f -e trace=process -- /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I launcher.py. Match the pre/post-exec PID; verify normal exit 7 and launch failure 127. These are program-selected codes, not a universal exec-error encoding. Keep the trace showing process creation, execve and wait4; Linux's fork wrapper may use clone.
traps: Expecting the parent to run first after fork, or treating a sleep as a synchronization guarantee.
Returning through normal Python cleanup after a failed child exec. Use os._exit for this post-fork failure path and collect the result in the parent.
Extending this single-threaded fork pattern to a multithreaded runtime. Copied locks can remain owned by threads that no longer exist in the child.

selfTest.q: Does successful exec return zero to the old program?
selfTest.a: No. It does not return. Only failure returns to the old image; the kernel keeps the process identity but installs a new program image.

selfTest.q: What must happen after a blocked child's I/O completes before it executes again?
selfTest.a: It becomes runnable and the scheduler must select it. Completion does not imply immediate execution.

selfTest.q: Is every system call a context switch?
selfTest.a: No. It changes privilege mode, but another task need not run. A blocked call can lead to a context switch.

selfTest.q: Can the raw wait status be compared directly with exit code 7?
selfTest.a: No. First test normal exit with WIFEXITED and then decode WEXITSTATUS. Signaled termination has a different interpretation.

practice.name: OSTEP process-run.py: CPU/I/O state prediction
practice.locator: README Overview and process-run.py; use -s 1 and -s 2 with -l 5:50,5:100 -L 5
practice.note: Predict the full trace before adding -c -p. Compare SWITCH_ON_IO with SWITCH_ON_END and IO_RUN_LATER with IO_RUN_IMMEDIATE. The answer flag is the simulator's oracle, not a Linux scheduler test. Save one matching local launcher trace for the section evidence pack.

units.stopWhen: Your launcher reaps both success and exec-failure children, and your two-seed simulator predictions distinguish blocked time from ready time and a mode switch from a task switch.

fit.note: OSTEP provides process mechanisms and scheduling assumptions, AlgoMaster provides launch edge cases, and the named simulator plus a local traced launcher meet implement depth without an unavailable xv6 toolchain.

Distinguish signal notification, delivery, termination and status collection.

study.title: Wait status and child states
study.locator: DESCRIPTION: wait() and waitpid(), status macros, waitid() and WNOWAIT; NOTES on zombies

study.title: Offsets shared through fork and dup
study.locator: Chapter 39, Sections 39.4 to 39.6, especially Shared File Table Entries: fork() And dup()

focus: A descriptor entry holds its own close-on-exec flag; the open file description holds the shared offset and status flags. A repeated open creates independent open state.
After dup2, close unused pipe endpoints in both processes. EOF requires an empty pipe and no remaining write references; parent exit is not the definition of EOF.
Signals have dispositions and per-thread masks. SIGCHLD can coalesce; drain waitable children rather than counting notifications.
A zombie has already released its user memory and descriptors. An orphan changes parent; Linux can adopt it through a subreaper rather than the host PID 1.
units.reproduce:
Write a Python parent with two os.pipe pairs. Fork one child, dup2 its request-read end onto fd 0 and response-write end onto fd 1, close all original endpoints and execl /bin/cat. In the parent close the child-only ends, write b'abc
' with a partial-write loop, close the request writer, read the response until EOF and waitpid the child. Assert exactly b'abc
' and normal exit 0. Run strace -f -e trace=process,pipe,pipe2,dup2,read,write,close -- /home/saisandeshk/Study/Learn/ai-atlas-work/pyenv-prog/bin/python -I pipes.py. In a separate empty pipe, set the reader nonblocking: retaining the writer gives BlockingIOError, closing the last writer gives b''. Finally fork a child that sets SIGTERM to SIG_DFL, announces readiness through a pipe and waits; signal it only after readiness. Use waitid with WEXITED|WNOWAIT to observe /proc/<pid>/status state Z, then waitpid and verify WIFSIGNALED with WTERMSIG==SIGTERM. Use no sleep as an ordering guarantee.
traps: Keeping a spare write descriptor open and waiting for EOF forever. Inheritance and duplication both retain references.
Assuming Python's newly created descriptors survive exec. They are non-inheritable by default; deliberate dup2 onto standard I/O is inheritable unless requested otherwise.
Calling arbitrary logging or allocation from a native signal handler, or assuming shell status 128+signal is the raw wait status.

selfTest.q: A child reads through an inherited regular-file descriptor. Does the parent's offset advance?
selfTest.a: Yes, if both entries still refer to the same inherited open file description. Separate open calls would have independent offsets.

selfTest.q: The producer exited, but an unrelated child inherited its pipe writer. Will an empty pipe return EOF?
selfTest.a: No. A write reference still exists. A blocking reader waits and a nonblocking reader reports EAGAIN until the last writer closes.

selfTest.q: Why does one SIGCHLD handler invocation not imply one terminated child?
selfTest.a: Standard signals can coalesce and SIGCHLD can report other child state changes. Reap in a loop with waitpid(-1, ..., WNOHANG), handling the documented return cases.

selfTest.q: Can SIGKILL remove a zombie's retained status record?
selfTest.a: No. It is already terminated. Its parent or adopter must collect the record; signal delivery is not reaping.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a supervised pipe worker with a descriptor ownership diagram, deliberate leaked-writer regression test, signal termination, zombie observation, and guaranteed closure and reaping on success and failure.
units.stopWhen: The pipe round trip passes, your nonblocking leak test distinguishes EAGAIN from EOF, and your signal test observes then reaps the zombie with a correctly decoded wait status.

fit.note: OSTEP and the selected AlgoMaster descriptor, signal and zombie lessons explain owned kernel state; wait(2) supplies the precise observation contract and the mini-project supplies implementation practice.
